name: Going Concern Analysis
title: Going Concern Analysis
answer: Going concern analysis in continuous audit and assurance assesses whether a company can meet its obligations for at least twelve months from the reporting date. It covers liquidity, solvency, covenant compliance, management plans, and external conditions such as credit availability or supply chain stress. Continuous audit shifts this from an annual judgment to an ongoing monitoring activity, with AI flagging changes in financial health between reporting periods.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Going concern analysis in continuous audit and assurance assesses whether a company can meet its obligations for at least twelve months from the reporting date. It covers liquidity, solvency, covenant compliance, management plans, and external conditions such as credit availability or supply chain stress. Continuous audit shifts this from an annual judgment to an ongoing monitoring activity, with AI flagging changes in financial health between reporting periods.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on integrated data pipelines that draw from ERP systems, bank and credit feeds, market data, news, and regulatory filings. Cloud-based analytics platforms store this data in secure, access-controlled environments and feed it into scoring and alerting workflows. The infrastructure must preserve data lineage so that every signal can be traced back to its source document or transaction.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Models are configured to score liquidity ratios, cash flow forecasts, covenant headroom, and the tone of going concern language in disclosures. Anomaly detection flags sudden changes in payment behavior, supplier terms, or management commentary that may indicate financial distress. Human auditors review the model outputs, set thresholds for alerts, and combine them with professional judgment before forming a conclusion.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: AI going concern signals can influence audit opinions and lending decisions, so model provenance, data lineage, and auditability are central concerns. Risks include false positives that damage a viable company, missed warnings from incomplete data, and overreliance on automated scores. Professional standards require the auditor to retain responsibility for the judgment, with AI treated as evidence rather than a conclusion, and documentation must show how the model was used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous going concern monitoring with real-time cash flow and covenant alerts integrated into audit and board reporting. Generative AI is likely to be used more for drafting and challenging going concern assessments, while regulators clarify expectations for model validation and disclosure. The goal is earlier warning and more defensible, evidence-backed judgments without replacing auditor accountability.
